extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional politics; reformers and practitioners interested in parliamentary government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and standards for when and how a parliamentary House (specifically the House of Commons) can function well — covering composition of representatives, constituency design, legislative and selection functions, and alignment with public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative moderation and freedom from class prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: A parliamentary government is possible only when the overwhelming majority of the representatives are men essentially moderate, of no marked varieties, free from class prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representatives are immoderate or strongly factionalised the assembly will elect immoderate ministries and enact violent laws; the mass of Parliament ought to be men of moderate sentiments to preserve parliamentary government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory (geographical) constituencies vs voluntary constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Two modes of making constituencies: (1) the law may make them (compulsory constituencies, e.g., geographical divisions) or (2) the law may leave electors to group themselves (voluntary constituencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues compulsory constituencies are necessary and voluntary constituencies destructive. Voluntary constituencies throw minority votes into useful combinations but produce organised constituency-making, party manipulation, and despotism; therefore law-made, geographical constituencies preserve independence and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional transferability of votes is ruinous
rubrics_metrics.description: The optional transferability of votes (allowing voters to transfer votes or form self-chosen constituencies) is not a salutary aid, but a ruinous innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such transferability encourages registration/manipulation organisations, caucuses, and wire-pullers, producing party-dominated, enslaved members and frequent electoral instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constituency-making as a trade (organisation and manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If constituencies are voluntarily composed, constituency-making becomes a trade: organised managers will allocate voters and create 'full' constituencies, producing member-makers who prefer subservience over independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: American presidential caucus dynamics; registration associations that steer late voters to pre-selected cards. Resulting anti-patterns include tightened party fetters, diminished member independence, and latent wire-pullers controlling representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members must have extrinsic independence and inherent moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two necessary conditions for parliamentary government: extrinsic independence (members not enslaved to apparatus/constituency-makers) and inherent moderation of members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary constituencies, caucuses, and frequent elections undermine extrinsic independence; ensuring independence helps Parliament resist factional pressures and maintain deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five core functions the House must perform well
rubrics_metrics.description: A House of Commons must perform five functions well: it must elect a ministry well, legislate well, teach the nation well, express the nation's will well, and bring matters to the nation's attention well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five are presented as the tests of a working House; each function can be judged by how well Parliament aligns with and serves the nation's opinion and needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electing a ministry according to national opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The choosing/selecting business of Parliament should select rulers as the nation wishes; free government is judged by the English nation here and now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Parliament chose ministers detested by the nation, an organised popular grievance would promptly overturn them. Parliamentary selection is 'well' when it mirrors public opinion despite party divisions; the Palmerston example shows Parliament can align with the national will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation should correspond to the nation's wishes and avoid poor legislative machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should pass laws as the nation wishes to have them passed, but the machinery for detailed legislation (e.g., committee of the whole House dealing with elaborate clauses) is defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee-of-the-whole practice can wedge irrelevant clauses into Acts; subject to two considerable defects (noted elsewhere), Parliament generally enacts legislation in accordance with public opinion but legislative procedure needs improvement to avoid ad hoc or misplaced clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament should express the nation's opinion well (the 'lyrical' function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should be able to express, in words, the characteristic heart of the nation — especially on foreign matters where legislation cannot remedy events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'lyrical' function is valuable: even if opinion is incomplete or erroneous, a free nation's distinctive judgments may contain cardinal truths helpful internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament should elevate public opinion (teaching) — current shortcoming
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Parliament's functions is to teach and elevate public opinion; the author regards this as the task Parliament does worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Parliament expresses public opinion, it often fails to improve or elevate it; recognizing and remedying this shortcoming is part of improving parliamentary performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive weight to the landed interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament leans too much to the opinions of the landed interest; examples like the Cattle Plague Act show hurried, despot-like handling when landed incomes were threatened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The landed gentry are numerous, socially bonded, and often locally chosen (counties electing only local landowners), giving them disproportionate influence; this bias should be corrected to prevent partial legislation favoring landed interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must reflect present economic/population realities (weight growing districts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existing parliamentary structure gives too little weight to growing districts of the country and too much to regions of past greatness; representation should follow present wealth and importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial and manufacturing regions (the North) are increasing in importance while traditional southern counties decline; reform aims to give more power to growing districts and reduce overrepresentation of historically important but now-stationary regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of Parliaments (term length vs. constituency pressures)
rubrics_metrics.description: If constituencies are self-formed and eager, they will demand frequent elections and short-lived Parliaments; long terms (e.g., septennial Parliaments) help preserve member independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary, earnest constituencies would push for annual or frequent elections, undermining the stabilising effect of longer terms; appropriate term length is part of preserving extrinsic independence and effective government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Parliament may include aristocratic elements without betraying public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of persons of aristocratic descent in Parliament does not necessarily impair its accordance with public opinion; the English aristocracy are not a caste apart and reflect propertied opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining some aristocratic element can help 'match' the dignified and efficient parts of polity; deferential instincts in constituencies often favour titled candidates, and this is not inherently contrary to representing public opinion.
